questions.text: To talk about past holidays, we use the :
questions.explanation: Finished past events take the past simple: "Last holiday, I visited my grandmother in the village." Regular verbs take -ed; irregular verbs have special forms (go → went).

questions.text: The past form of "go" is :
questions.explanation: go is irregular: go → went (past simple) → gone (past participle). Other examples: see → saw, eat → ate, swim → swam, travel → travelled.

questions.text: Which question asks about past holidays ?
options: Did you visit the beach last year ?
questions.explanation: Past simple questions use Did + subject + base verb (no -ed on the main verb): "Did you enjoy your holidays?"

questions.text: "Last holiday, we ___ to the seaside." Choose the correct verb :
questions.explanation: "Last holiday" indicates a finished past → past simple: travelled (regular verb, -ed).

questions.text: True or False : Holiday activities vocabulary includes swimming, fishing, visiting grandparents and playing with friends.
questions.explanation: Typical holiday activities: to swim, to fish, to visit relatives, to play games, to travel, to rest — all useful to describe your vacations.

questions.text: To describe a past habit we no longer do, we use :
questions.explanation: "Used to + verb" expresses a past habit or state that has stopped: "I used to play football every evening at primary school."

questions.text: The negative form of "I used to walk to school" is :
questions.explanation: Negative : didn't + use to (no -d!): "I didn't use to like English but now I do." Same for questions: "Did you use to…?"

questions.text: "I ___ be afraid of teachers, but now I'm not." Complete :
questions.explanation: Affirmative form = used to + infinitive. "I used to be afraid" = a past state that no longer exists.

questions.text: School memories vocabulary includes :
questions.explanation: School memories: boarding school (internat), schoolmates (camarades), playground (cour de récréation), classrooms, strict teachers, games.

questions.text: True or False : "Used to" can describe both past habits (I used to play) and past states (I used to be shy).
questions.explanation: Used to works with action verbs (habits) AND state verbs (be, like, live): "I used to live in Bouaké" = a state that has changed.

questions.text: A first conditional sentence (real condition) is formed with :
questions.explanation: If + present simple → will + infinitive: "If you work hard, you will pass your exams." The condition is possible/real.

questions.text: "If you don't study, you ___ fail." Complete :
questions.explanation: Negative consequence: will not → won't: "If you don't study, you won't pass your BEPC."

questions.text: School results vocabulary includes :
options: Pass, fail, succeed, get good marks
questions.explanation: Results vocabulary: to pass (réussir), to fail (échouer), to succeed (réussir), to get good/bad marks, to work hard, to be lazy.

questions.text: "If it rains, we ___ at home." Choose :
questions.explanation: First conditional: if + present → will + infinitive: "If it rains, we will stay at home." The main clause carries the future.

questions.text: True or False : In a conditional sentence, "will" never goes in the if-clause.
questions.explanation: Rule: "will" belongs to the main clause, never after "if": say "If you work, you will succeed" NOT ✗ "If you will work…".

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U2L1_Rural_women.title: Rural women — can/be able to, reported speech

questions.text: To express ability in the present, we use :
questions.explanation: "Rural women can cultivate rice" = ability. "Be able to" is more flexible: it works in all tenses (was able to, will be able to).

questions.text: Rural women's activities include :
options: Farming, selling at the market, fetching water, cooking
questions.explanation: Vocabulary: to farm/cultivate, to sell at the market, to fetch water (puiser l'eau), to cook, to take care of children, to harvest.

questions.text: Direct → indirect speech: "I am tired," she says →
questions.explanation: In indirect speech, the pronoun adapts to the speaker: "I" becomes "she". The tense stays the same if the reporting verb is in the present (says).

questions.text: "She can sell her products at the market" means she :
questions.explanation: Can = ability or possibility: she is able to sell / it is possible for her to sell.

questions.text: True or False : "be able to" can replace "can" in all tenses: was able to (past), will be able to (future).
questions.explanation: "Can" has no infinitive or future form: for other tenses we use "be able to": yesterday I was able to finish; tomorrow I will be able to go.

questions.text: Women's rights include :
options: The right to vote, to education, to work and to own property
questions.explanation: Rights vocabulary: the right to education (droit à l'éducation), the right to vote (droit de vote), the right to work, the right to own property (propriété), equality.

questions.text: "Equality" means :
options: Having the same rights and opportunities
questions.explanation: Equality (égalité) = same rights, same chances for men and women. Opposite: inequality/discrimination.

questions.text: "Girls must go to school" expresses :
questions.explanation: "Must" expresses obligation: sending girls to school is a duty and a right, not a choice.

questions.text: A synonym of "to fight for rights" is :
options: to defend / to struggle for rights
questions.explanation: To fight for / to defend / to struggle for rights = lutter pour les droits. Related vocabulary: freedom, justice, discrimination, empower.

questions.text: True or False : Promoting women's rights helps the development of the whole country.
questions.explanation: Educated and empowered women contribute to the economy, to children's education and to health: women's rights benefit the entire society.

questions.text: To give an opinion, we say :
options: I think that… / In my opinion…
questions.explanation: Opinion phrases: "I think (that)…", "In my opinion…", "I believe…", "For me…". Example: "I think girls should stay at school."

questions.text: The comparative of superiority of a short adjective is :
questions.explanation: Short adjectives: + -er + than: "Boys are taller than girls at this age." Long adjectives take "more…than": "more important than".

questions.text: The comparative of equality is formed with :
questions.explanation: "as + adjective + as" = aussi… que : "Girls are as intelligent as boys." Negative: "not as/so…as" = pas aussi… que.

questions.text: "Education is as important for girls ___ for boys." Complete :
questions.explanation: Equality: as…as. "Girls' schooling is as important as boys'" — equal importance.

questions.text: True or False : For long adjectives (3+ syllables), the comparative uses "more … than".
questions.explanation: Long adjectives: more + adjective + than: "more important than", "more difficult than". Never "importanter"!

questions.text: To say how we travel, we use :
options: by + transport name (by bus, by car, by train)
questions.explanation: "by + moyen de transport" (no article): by bus, by taxi, by plane, by canoe. Exceptions: on foot, on a bike/motorbike, in a car (when specified: "in my father's car").

questions.text: Means of transport in Côte d'Ivoire include :
options: Gbaka, woro-woro, moto-taxi, bus, canoe, plane
questions.explanation: Local means of transport: gbaka (minibus), woro-woro (taxi communal), moto-taxi, bus, ferry, canoe (pirogue), taxi, private car, bicycle, plane.

questions.text: To express a wish politely, we say :
options: I want to travel / I would like to travel
questions.explanation: "I want to" = je veux (direct); "I would like to" = j'aimerais (poli). Example: "I would like to travel by plane."

questions.text: « Je vais à l'école à pied » =
options: I go to school by foot
I go to school on foot
I go to school in foot
I go to school with foot
questions.explanation: Walking = "on foot" (fixed expression, never "by foot"). Other movements: by bike/on a bike, by bus, by taxi.

questions.text: True or False : "by" is used with the general means of transport (by bus), but "on" or "in" is used when the vehicle is specified (in my father's car, on my bike).
questions.explanation: Rule: by + vehicle (general, no article) vs in/on + determiner + vehicle (specific): "I came by car" vs "I came in my uncle's car".

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U3L2_Travel_plane.title: Travelling by plane — necessity and preferences

questions.text: Airport vocabulary includes :
options: Ticket, passport, boarding pass, luggage, flight
questions.explanation: At the airport: ticket (billet), passport (passeport), boarding pass (carte d'embarquement), luggage/baggage (bagages), flight (vol), to check in (enregistrer), departure/arrival.

questions.text: To express necessity, we use :
questions.explanation: "need to + verb" = avoir besoin de : "You need to check in two hours before the flight." Negative: "don't need to" = pas nécessaire.

questions.text: To express a preference between two options, we say :
options: I prefer travelling by plane to travelling by road
questions.explanation: Prefer X to Y = préférer X à Y : "I prefer the plane to the bus because it is faster." Also: "I like… better than…" / "I'd rather…".

questions.text: "You ___ to show your passport at the boarding gate." Complete :
questions.explanation: need to + infinitive: "You need to show your passport" = tu dois présenter ton passeport.

questions.text: True or False : "prefer … to …" never takes "than".
questions.explanation: Say "I prefer planes to trains" — never "prefer…than…"! Alternative form: "I would rather fly than take the bus" (would rather + infinitive…than…).

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U3L3_New_life_UK.title: A new life in the UK — reported speech and past simple

questions.text: In reported speech, "She said she was happy" reports the direct sentence :
questions.explanation: Direct : "I am happy," she said. Indirect : she said (that) she was happy — the tense moves back one step (am → was) because the reporting verb is in the past.

questions.text: When the reporting verb is in the past (said), the present simple becomes :
questions.explanation: Backshift: present → past (am → was, live → lived); past simple → past perfect (lived → had lived); will → would; can → could.

questions.text: Living abroad vocabulary includes :
options: to settle, to adapt, homesickness, a new culture
questions.explanation: Vocabulary: to settle (s'installer), to adapt to (s'adapter), homesickness (mal du pays), culture shock, foreign (étranger), newcomer (nouveau venu).

questions.text: « Il a dit qu'il vivait à Londres » in indirect speech :
options: He said he lives in London
He said he lived in London
He says he lived in London
questions.explanation: said (past) → backshift: lives → lived. "He said he lived in London."

questions.text: True or False : The past simple describes finished actions at a definite past time (yesterday, last year, in 2020).
questions.explanation: Past simple = completed action + finished time marker: "I arrived in the UK in 2020." With an unfinished time (this week, ever, already) → present perfect.

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U4L1_Fashion_wear.title: Fashion — present simple vs present continuous

questions.text: The present continuous describes :
questions.explanation: Present continuous (be + V-ing) = action en cours : "She is wearing a red dress today." Present simple = habit/fact : "She wears nice clothes."

questions.text: Fashion vocabulary includes :
options: trendy, old-fashioned, to wear, outfit, style
questions.explanation: Fashion words: trendy (à la mode), old-fashioned (démodé), to wear (porter), outfit (tenue), style, elegant, casual, smart.

questions.text: "Look ! She ___ a beautiful pagne." Choose :
questions.explanation: "Look !" signals an action happening now → present continuous: is wearing (be + V-ing).

questions.text: "He always ___ elegant clothes." (habit) Choose :
questions.explanation: "Always" = habit → present simple, 3rd person -s : wears.

questions.text: True or False : "to wear" = porter (vêtement) ; the past is "wore" and the participle is "worn".
questions.explanation: Irregular verb : wear → wore → worn. "She wore a nice dress yesterday" / "This dress was worn by a queen."

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U4L2_Passive_fashion.title: Passive voice — describing how clothes are made

questions.text: The passive voice is formed with :
questions.explanation: Passive = subject + be (conjugated) + past participle : "Pagnes are made in Côte d'Ivoire." The doer is introduced by "by" (often omitted).

questions.text: Active : "Weavers make kente cloth." → Passive :
options: Kente cloth is made by weavers
Weavers are made by kente cloth
questions.explanation: The object (kente cloth) becomes the subject ; be + past participle (made) ; the agent follows "by".

questions.text: We use the passive when :
options: The action is less important than the doer
The doer is unknown, obvious or less important than the action/result
questions.explanation: The passive highlights the process or the product, not the person : "Cotton is grown in the north" (the growers are obvious/unimportant).

questions.text: "Used to" expresses :
options: A past habit or state that no longer exists
questions.explanation: "People used to wear traditional clothes more often" = habitude passée qui a changé.

questions.text: True or False : "This pagne was woven by hand" is a passive sentence in the past.
questions.explanation: was (past of be) + woven (past participle of weave) = passive past. The agent is "by hand" (à la main).

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U4L3_Success_story.title: A success story — present perfect vs past simple

questions.text: The present perfect links :
options: A past action to the present (result visible now)
questions.explanation: have/has + past participle : the action is past but its result matters now : "She has become a famous designer" (she IS famous now).

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence for a finished, dated past action :
options: She has started her business in 2015
questions.explanation: With a finished time marker (in 2015, yesterday, last year), English uses the past simple — never the present perfect.

questions.text: Present perfect markers include :
options: already, just, ever, never, since, for
questions.explanation: Unfinished/linked-to-now markers → present perfect : "I have already sold 100 pagnes", "I have never been to Paris", "since 2015", "for 5 years".

questions.text: "She ___ (sell) 1 000 outfits since 2020." Choose :
questions.explanation: "since 2020" links past to present → present perfect : has sold.

questions.text: True or False : "for" indicates a duration (for ten years) ; "since" indicates a starting point (since 2014).
questions.explanation: for + durée (for 5 years, for two months) ; since + point de départ (since Monday, since 2014, since she was a child).

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U5L1_Wish_city.title: Wishes about the city — wish + past, used to

questions.text: To express a wish about the present (regret), we use :
questions.explanation: "I wish + past" = regret about the present : "I wish I lived in a cleaner city." (= malheureusement, ce n'est pas le cas).

questions.text: "I wish my city ___ less polluted." Complete :
questions.explanation: After "I wish", use the past tense for a present regret : "I wish my city were cleaner" (were preferred for all persons in formal English).

questions.text: "There used to be" expresses :
options: Something that existed before but no longer does
questions.explanation: "There used to be a forest here, but now there are buildings" = comparaison passé/présent : ce qui existait avant a disparu.

questions.text: City vocabulary includes :
options: traffic jam, pollution, slum, skyscraper, crowded
questions.explanation: City words : traffic jam (embouteillage), pollution, slum (bidonville), skyscraper (gratte-ciel), crowded (bondé), noise, public transport.

questions.text: True or False : "I wish I were rich" and "I wish I was rich" are both heard ; "were" is the more formal form.
questions.explanation: After "I wish", "were" applies to all persons in careful English (subjunctive) : "I wish I were a bird." In everyday speech, "was" is also accepted.

questions.text: To express feelings, we use the structure :
questions.explanation: "feel + adjective" : I feel happy/sad/tired/lonely/safe. "In the village, people feel safe and peaceful."

questions.text: Village life vocabulary includes :
options: peaceful, quiet, farming, close-knit community, fresh air
questions.explanation: Village words : peaceful (paisible), quiet (calme), farming (agriculture), community (communauté), fresh air, friendly neighbours ; opposites of city life.

questions.text: The question "___ do you like village life ? — Because it is quiet." uses :
questions.explanation: "Why…?" asks for a reason ; the answer begins with "Because…".

questions.text: "___ people live in this village ? — About 500." Complete :
questions.explanation: How many + countable noun (people, houses) ; how much + uncountable (water, time, money).

questions.text: True or False : Comparing village and city : "The village is quieter than the city, but the city is more exciting."
questions.explanation: Correct comparatives : quiet → quieter (-er for short adjective) ; exciting → more exciting (long adjective). Both forms are grammatically right.

questions.text: "The city is so noisy that I can't sleep" expresses :
questions.explanation: "so + adjective + that" = tellement… que : it introduces the consequence of a quality : so noisy → can't sleep.

questions.text: "so + adjective + that" : choose the correct sentence :
options: The village was so beautiful that we stayed a week
The village that was so beautiful
questions.explanation: Structure : so + adjective + that + clause : "so beautiful that we stayed a week" = si beau que nous sommes restés une semaine.

questions.text: With an adverb, the structure becomes :
options: so + adverb + that : "He ran so fast that nobody could catch him"
questions.explanation: so + adverb + that : "so fast", "so slowly", "so well" — the rule is the same : so + adverb + that + consequence.

questions.text: Rural exodus vocabulary includes :
options: to leave the village, to migrate, to look for jobs
questions.explanation: Rural exodus : people leave the countryside for the city → migrate (migrer), look for jobs (chercher du travail), overcrowding (surpeuplement), opportunity (opportunité).

questions.text: True or False : « Il est si pauvre qu'il ne peut pas payer l'école » = "He is so poor that he can't pay for school."
questions.explanation: Correct translation of the cause-consequence structure : so + adjective (poor) + that + result clause.

questions.text: To make a polite request, we say :
options: Can/Could I have my ID card, please ?
questions.explanation: Polite requests : "Can I…?", "Could I…?", "May I…?" + please. "Could" is more polite than "can".

questions.text: "must" expresses :
questions.explanation: must = obligation forte : "You must respect the law." Opposite : mustn't = interdiction : "You mustn't steal."

questions.text: "mustn't" means :
questions.explanation: mustn't = interdit : "You mustn't cheat in exams." Careful : "don't have to" = no necessity (not forbidden, just not necessary).

questions.text: Rights vocabulary includes :
options: the right to education, to health, to vote, an ID card, a birth certificate
questions.explanation: Documents/rights : birth certificate (acte de naissance), ID card (carte d'identité), the right to… (droit à/de), freedom, justice.

questions.text: True or False : "You mustn't litter here" means littering is forbidden.
questions.explanation: mustn't = prohibition : "You mustn't litter" = il est interdit de jeter des ordures. Compare : "You don't have to litter" = pas nécessaire (but not forbidden).

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U6L2_Duties.title: Duties — have to / don't have to

questions.text: To express duties, we use :
questions.explanation: "have to + verb" = devoir (external obligation) : "Citizens have to pay taxes." "must" = strong/moral duty : "We must respect our parents."

questions.text: A citizen's duties include :
options: Paying taxes, respecting the law, voting, protecting the environment
questions.explanation: Duties vocabulary : to pay taxes (payer des impôts), to respect the law, to vote, to go to school, to protect the environment, to be honest.

questions.text: "You don't have to come early" means :
options: It is not necessary to come early
questions.explanation: "don't have to" = absence of necessity (pas obligé), NOT a prohibition. Compare : mustn't = interdiction.

questions.text: "She ___ go to school every day" (obligation). Choose :
questions.explanation: 3rd person singular : has to. "She has to go to school" = elle doit aller à l'école.

questions.text: True or False : "mustn't" and "don't have to" have the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Different : mustn't = forbidden (interdit) ; don't have to = not necessary (pas obligé, mais possible). Example : "You don't have to wear a uniform on Friday."

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U6L3_Tolerance.title: Tolerance — obligation with have got to

questions.text: Tolerance means :
options: Accepting and respecting differences (religion, ethnicity, opinions)
questions.explanation: Tolerance = respect and acceptance of differences : peaceful coexistence (coexistence pacifique). Opposite : intolerance, hatred (haine).

questions.text: "have got to" expresses :
questions.explanation: "I've got to go" = "I have to go" = je dois partir (obligation). More common in spoken British English : "We've got to be tolerant."

questions.text: Peace vocabulary includes :
questions.explanation: Peace vocabulary : peace (paix), respect, harmony (harmonie), coexistence, dialogue, brotherhood (fraternité), non-violence, understanding.

questions.text: "We ___ respect other people's beliefs." (obligation) Choose :
options: have got to / must / have to
questions.explanation: All three express obligation : "We must / have to / have got to respect other people's beliefs" = nous devons respecter les croyances des autres.

questions.text: True or False : Tolerance contributes to social peace and national unity.
questions.explanation: A tolerant society accepts differences and lives in peace : dialogue instead of conflict → national unity and development.

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U7L1_Avoid_diseases.title: Avoiding diseases — should, passive voice, malaria

questions.text: To give advice, we use :
questions.explanation: should = conseil : "You should sleep under a mosquito net." shouldn't = déconseillé : "You shouldn't drink dirty water."

questions.text: Malaria is transmitted by :
options: The bite of the female Anopheles mosquito
questions.explanation: Malaria (paludisme) is caused by the Plasmodium parasite, inoculated by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. Prevention : mosquito nets, eliminating stagnant water.

questions.text: Passive : "Malaria ___ by mosquitoes." Choose :
questions.explanation: Passive = be + past participle : "is transmitted" (present passive). The agent follows "by".

questions.text: Health vocabulary includes :
options: disease, fever, mosquito net, prevention, treatment
questions.explanation: Health words : disease (maladie), fever (fièvre), mosquito net (moustiquaire), prevention, treatment (traitement), symptoms, to fall ill (tomber malade), hygiene.

questions.text: True or False : "Stagnant water should be eliminated around houses" is a passive sentence giving advice.
questions.explanation: should + be + past participle = passive advice : "should be eliminated" = devrait être éliminée. Common in prevention messages.

Fiche_ANG_4eme_U7L2_School_clean.title: Keeping the school clean — opinions and suggestions

questions.text: To express an opinion, we say :
options: I think (that)… / In my opinion… / I believe…
questions.explanation: Opinion starters : "I think (that) our school is clean", "In my opinion…", "I believe that…", "For me…".

questions.text: To make a suggestion, we say :
options: Why don't we clean the classroom ? / Let's clean ! / How about cleaning ?
questions.explanation: Suggestions : "Why don't we/you + verb…?", "Let's + verb", "How about + -ing", "We could + verb". All propose an action politely.

questions.text: Hygiene vocabulary at school includes :
options: to sweep, to dust, a dustbin, to litter, a broom
questions.explanation: Hygiene words : to sweep (balayer), to dust (épousseter), dustbin (poubelle), to litter (jeter des ordures), broom (balai), clean (propre) / dirty (sale).

questions.text: « Pourquoi ne pas balayer la cour ? » =
options: Why don't we sweep the yard ?
questions.explanation: "Why don't we + infinitive" = pourquoi ne pas… : "Why don't we sweep the yard ?" — classic suggestion form.

questions.text: True or False : Good hygiene at school prevents diseases and creates a better learning environment.
questions.explanation: A clean school = fewer diseases (less malaria, diarrhoea, infections) and a pleasant environment where students learn better.
